extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, diplomats, and general readers learning to detect stereotypes and evaluate public arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying and critiquing stereotypes, moral codes, and coded assumptions in public opinion, propaganda, and political argument. Emphasizes practical clues (contradiction, space, time) and the need to interrogate underlying assumptions about human nature and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is a mix of fact and expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The way we see things is a combination of what is there and of what we expected to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reports or claims, ask which parts of the perception come from observation and which from pre-existing images or expectations. Examples: mistaking a stranger for a friend from a hat or gait; different reactions to the same page of Kant by differing philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise increases discriminations but can entrench stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness multiplies the number of aspects we are prepared to discover, plus the habit of discounting our expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether claimed expertise genuinely broadens perception or simply supplies more detailed stereotypes that exclude contrary facts. Example: specialists see distinctions unseen by laypeople, but partial expertness can exaggerate fitting facts into a stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for selective attention and confirmation (stereotype-driven evidence selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a system of stereotypes is well fixed, attention is called to facts which support it and diverted from those which contradict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether arguments marshal evidence that fits a preferred model while ignoring contradictory data. Historical example: rival accounts of trusts where each side publishes statistics and anecdotes to prove opposite claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogate codes for their implicit assumptions about facts
rubrics_metrics.description: At the core of every moral code there is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history; the rules apply to that imagined situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what assumptions about human motives, institutions, and history underlie a moral, political, or economic code. Compare, for instance, patriotic vs commercial codes which assume different human natures and thus prescribe different behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypothesis-based views from dogmatic myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes under the influence of science treat conceptions as hypotheses open to proof or contradiction; myths accept conceptions without question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a belief-system allows testing and revision or treats its premises as inviolate. A myth may contain truth but lacks the critical power to separate truth from error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect internal contradictions as a clue to constructed stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of contradictions in the principles used to justify claims often shows that different stereotypes are being invoked to obliterate inconvenient facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mutually contradictory principles being deployed in sequence (e.g., geographic, historic, defensive, reparational claims all used to justify territorial demands). Such contradiction suggests argument constructed to defend a pre-decided claim rather than to find truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check spatial/logistical feasibility (inability to take account of space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that ignore practical geography or transportation confuse map-geometry with real-world logistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether proposed actions are feasible given distances, transport, and on-the-ground barriers. Example: demands to re-establish an 'eastern front' without accounting for 5,000 miles and a broken railway between Vladivostok and Poland show failure to account for space; frontier lines drawn purely by ethnic map may cut through factories or churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check temporal perspective and appropriate time-conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims often err by applying the wrong time-horizon; a wise judgment distinguishes the proper time-conception for the issue at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the decision or policy is being evaluated on appropriate short-term or long-term grounds. Examples: overly rigid wills or constitutions that attempt to control distant future behavior (perpetuities), and failures to recognize difference between immediate perceptual present and ideational/longer durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware use of absolute principles to censor context and escalate emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking an 'eternal principle' censors objections, isolates issues from context, and provokes strong emotions that make accommodation unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you see absolutist rhetoric (historic right, natural frontier, defense necessity) check whether it is silencing practical objections and inflaming sentiment rather than addressing concrete facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify villainization and conspiracy-mode explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition is often explained away by creating villains and alleging conspiracies, attributing complex social phenomena to organized plots or corrupt individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize claims that reduce diverse causes to single conspiracies (e.g., profiteers, capitalists, foreign agents). Such explanations are often compensatory mechanisms to preserve a preferred stereotype and avoid reassessing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize affective loading: judgments often precede evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are loaded with preference, affection, dislike, fears, and hopes; often a judgment (good/bad) exists prior to examination of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note emotional language and pre-judgments in an argument; insist on separating sentiment from evidence and testing whether feelings are driving perceived 'facts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice intellectual humility: consider that disagreement may be perceptual
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerance arises from recognizing opinions as partial experiences seen through stereotypes; opposing views may reflect different perceptions of facts rather than bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attributing perversity or dishonesty, ask whether the other party simply sees a different set of facts. Cultivate the habit of recognizing your own convictions as provisional and partly conditioned by stereotype.
